title: Rehearsing in the Dark: How Sleep Shapes What We Remember
skill_tip_en: For multi-step inference, link two separate statements in the text and choose the option that follows from both, rejecting any option that needs an extra assumption or an absolute word such as 'only' or 'all'.
paragraphs: For most of the twentieth century, sleep was widely regarded as a period of mental idleness, a nightly interruption during which the brain simply rested before the demands of the following day. That assumption has been steadily dismantled. A substantial body of research now indicates that sleep is not merely restorative but actively constructive: during the hours we spend unconscious, the brain appears to select, stabilise and reorganise the information it acquired while awake. This process, known as memory consolidation, may help to explain why a problem that seemed intractable in the evening sometimes looks surprisingly manageable the next morning.

The prevailing account of consolidation rests on a division of labour between two brain regions. The hippocampus, a small structure deep in the temporal lobe, is thought to capture new experiences rapidly but to store them only temporarily, rather like a notebook kept by the door. The neocortex, by contrast, learns slowly but retains information for years. According to the so-called active systems model, sleep provides the conditions under which memories are gradually transferred from the first store to the second. Crucially, this transfer is believed to occur not through passive decay but through repeated 'replay', in which patterns of neural activity recorded during learning are reactivated, often at many times their original speed.

Different stages of sleep seem to contribute in different ways. Deep, slow-wave sleep, which dominates the early part of the night, has been most closely linked to the strengthening of factual knowledge, such as word lists or the locations of objects. Rapid eye movement (REM) sleep, which becomes more frequent towards morning, has been associated instead with emotional memory and with the ability to detect hidden patterns in information. Because these stages are unevenly distributed across the night, a person who habitually sleeps for only five hours does not simply lose a proportional share of each; they lose a disproportionate amount of the later, REM-rich period.

Some of the most persuasive evidence comes from experiments in which memories are deliberately reactivated during sleep. In a 2023 study at a university in north-eastern Thailand, Dr. Pornthip Wongsakul and her colleagues taught 64 volunteers the positions of 40 images on a screen, with each image paired with a distinctive sound. While participants were in slow-wave sleep, half of the sounds were quietly replayed. The next morning, volunteers recalled the locations of the cued images noticeably more accurately than those of the uncued ones, even though none of them reported having heard anything during the night. The technique, called targeted memory reactivation, implies that consolidation can be steered, at least to some degree, towards particular memories.

Admittedly, the picture is less tidy than early enthusiasts suggested. Many of the effects reported in laboratory studies are modest, and several prominent findings have proved difficult to replicate with larger samples. Much of the research has also relied on artificial tasks, such as memorising unrelated word pairs, which bear little resemblance to the complex, meaningful learning that students actually undertake. Moreover, sleep is hard to isolate experimentally: participants who are deprived of sleep are also more tired, more stressed and less motivated when they are tested, so their poor performance may reflect their state at retrieval rather than any failure of consolidation itself.

A further complication concerns age. Older adults typically spend far less time in slow-wave sleep than young people do, and some researchers have proposed that this decline contributes to age-related memory loss. The evidence here is mostly correlational, however, and it remains unclear whether improving deep sleep in later life would restore memory or whether both changes stem from a common underlying cause. Trials using gentle acoustic stimulation, in which soft pulses of sound are timed to coincide with slow brain waves, have produced encouraging but inconsistent results.

Even so, the practical implications are difficult to ignore. If consolidation depends on sleep, then the familiar student habit of sacrificing rest in order to cram before an examination may be self-defeating, since material studied late into the night is precisely the material that is given the least opportunity to stabilise. Spreading study across several days, each followed by a full night's sleep, appears to be a more efficient strategy. Short daytime naps may offer a partial benefit, although they rarely contain much REM sleep. Ultimately, the research suggests that learning does not end when we close the book; a considerable part of it may take place only after we have switched off the light.

questions.q: What is the passage mainly about?
options: evidence that sleep actively stabilises memories, and the limits of that evidence
the reasons why scientists now regard sleep as a time of complete mental rest
a new treatment that can reverse memory loss in older adults through sound
the advantages of daytime naps over night-time sleep for university students
questions.explain: แนวคิดหลักอยู่ใน ¶1: “sleep is not merely restorative but actively constructive” จากนั้นบทความเสนอหลักฐาน (¶2–4) ข้อจำกัด (¶5–6) และข้อสรุปเชิงปฏิบัติ (¶7) จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก B ตรงข้ามกับความเชื่อเก่าที่ผู้เขียนบอกว่า “has been steadily dismantled” ส่วน C เกินจริง เพราะ ¶6 บอกว่าผลยัง “inconsistent”

questions.q: The author's remark that a difficult problem may look 'surprisingly manageable the next morning' (paragraph 1) suggests that
options: people generally think more intelligently in the morning than at night
rest without any mental activity is what makes problems seem easier
the brain may have continued to process the problem during sleep
most difficult problems can be solved only after a full night's sleep
questions.explain: ¶1 บอกว่าระหว่างหลับ สมอง “appears to select, stabilise and reorganise the information it acquired while awake” และกระบวนการนี้ “may help to explain” ว่าทำไมปัญหาดูง่ายขึ้นในตอนเช้า จึงอนุมานได้ว่าสมองยังทำงานกับปัญหาขณะหลับ (C) ตัวเลือก B เป็นกับดักเพราะคือมุมมองเก่าเรื่อง “mental idleness” ที่ผู้เขียนปฏิเสธ ส่วน D ใช้คำว่า only ซึ่งเกินกว่าข้อความ

questions.q: By comparing the hippocampus to 'a notebook kept by the door' (paragraph 2), the author implies that the hippocampus
options: retains information more reliably over time than the neocortex does
records new information quickly but is not meant to keep it permanently
is located near the outer surface of the brain rather than deep inside it
learns slowly but stores important memories for many years at a time
questions.explain: ¶2: ฮิปโปแคมปัส “capture new experiences rapidly but … store them only temporarily” สมุดจดข้างประตูจึงหมายถึงที่จดเร็วแต่ใช้ชั่วคราว (B) ตัวเลือก D เป็นคุณสมบัติของ neocortex ที่ “learns slowly but retains information for years” จึงเป็นการสลับสองส่วน และ C ตีความ 'by the door' ตามตัวอักษร ขัดกับ “deep in the temporal lobe”

questions.q: According to the active systems model described in paragraph 2, memories reach the neocortex mainly through
options: the gradual fading of the original trace stored in the hippocampus
the slow learning of new experiences that takes place while awake
a single rapid transfer that is completed early in the night
the repeated reactivation of activity patterns formed during learning
questions.explain: ¶2: การถ่ายโอนเกิด “not through passive decay but through repeated 'replay', in which patterns of neural activity recorded during learning are reactivated” จึงตอบ D ตัวเลือก A เป็นกับดักเพราะคือ passive decay ที่ข้อความปฏิเสธ ส่วน C ขัดกับคำว่า “repeated” และ “gradually”

questions.q: Which of the following can be inferred from paragraph 3 about a person who regularly sleeps for only five hours?
options: They lose an equal share of their slow-wave sleep and their REM sleep.
Their emotional memory is likely to suffer more than their recall of facts.
Their memory for word lists will be the most seriously affected ability.
They make up for lost REM sleep by having more of it early in the night.
questions.explain: ต้องเชื่อมสองข้อมูลใน ¶3: คนที่นอนห้าชั่วโมงเสีย “a disproportionate amount of the later, REM-rich period” และ REM เกี่ยวกับ “emotional memory” ขณะที่ slow-wave sleep ช่วงต้นคืนเกี่ยวกับความรู้เชิงข้อเท็จจริง จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก A ถูกปฏิเสธโดยตรง (“does not simply lose a proportional share”) ส่วน C กลับด้าน เพราะ word lists ผูกกับ slow-wave sleep ที่ยังได้อยู่

questions.q: What can be inferred from the fact that none of the volunteers in the 2023 study reported hearing anything during the night?
options: The memory benefit did not depend on participants being aware of the cues.
The sounds were too quiet to have had any measurable effect on the brain.
The volunteers had been woken up during REM sleep rather than deep sleep.
The cued images had been easier to memorise than the uncued ones at first.
questions.explain: ¶4: ภาพที่มีเสียงกระตุ้นถูกจำได้แม่นกว่า “even though none of them reported having heard anything” แสดงว่าผลดีเกิดขึ้นโดยผู้ร่วมวิจัยไม่รู้ตัว (A) ตัวเลือก B ขัดกับผลการทดลองที่มีผลจริง และ C ผิดเพราะเสียงถูกเล่น “in slow-wave sleep” ไม่ใช่ REM

questions.q: Why does the author point out in paragraph 5 that sleep-deprived participants are 'more tired, more stressed and less motivated'?
options: to explain how a lack of sleep physically damages the hippocampus
to argue that the tasks used in laboratory studies are too artificial
to show that poor test results may not be caused by weak consolidation
to prove that memory consolidation does not take place during sleep
questions.explain: ¶5: ผู้เขียนสรุปว่า “their poor performance may reflect their state at retrieval rather than any failure of consolidation itself” จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก B เป็นกับดักเพราะเป็นข้อจำกัดอีกข้อในย่อหน้าเดียวกัน แต่ไม่ใช่จุดประสงค์ของประโยคนี้ ส่วน D ใช้คำว่า prove ซึ่งรุนแรงเกินไป

questions.q: The author would most likely agree that the link between reduced slow-wave sleep and memory loss in older adults
options: has been firmly confirmed by trials using acoustic stimulation
explains why young people need less deep sleep than older adults
shows that age-related memory decline cannot be slowed at all
has not yet been shown to be a relationship of cause and effect
questions.explain: ¶6: หลักฐาน “is mostly correlational” และยังไม่ชัดว่า “both changes stem from a common underlying cause” หรือไม่ จึงยังพิสูจน์ความเป็นเหตุเป็นผลไม่ได้ (D) ตัวเลือก A เป็นกับดักเพราะการทดลองให้ผล “encouraging but inconsistent” ไม่ใช่ยืนยันแน่ชัด ส่วน B กลับข้อมูลที่ว่าผู้สูงอายุมี slow-wave sleep น้อยกว่า

questions.q: Based on paragraph 7, which plan would the author most likely recommend to a student with an important examination in one week?
options: studying intensively on the final night so the material is freshest
studying part of the material each day and sleeping fully every night
replacing night-time sleep with several short naps during the day
reviewing all of the material only once, immediately after waking up
questions.explain: ¶7: “Spreading study across several days, each followed by a full night's sleep, appears to be a more efficient strategy” จึงตอบ B ตัวเลือก A คือการอ่านหนักคืนสุดท้ายที่ผู้เขียนเรียกว่า “self-defeating” ส่วน C ผิดเพราะงีบกลางวันให้ประโยชน์เพียง “partial” และแทบไม่มี REM

questions.q: What name is given to the process by which the brain selects, stabilises and reorganises information during sleep? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶1: “This process, known as memory consolidation, may help to explain…” คำตอบคือ memory consolidation (การรวบรวมความจำให้มั่นคง)

questions.q: What is the name of the technique in which sounds linked to learning are replayed during sleep? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶4: “The technique, called targeted memory reactivation, implies that consolidation can be steered” คำตอบคือ targeted memory reactivation

questions.q: What method have trials used to try to deepen slow waves in older adults? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶6: “Trials using gentle acoustic stimulation, in which soft pulses of sound are timed to coincide with slow brain waves” คำตอบคือ (gentle) acoustic stimulation

title: Gardening the Reef: Hope, Hype and the Limits of Coral Restoration
skill_tip_en: Track the author's signal words, such as 'admittedly', 'to my mind', 'yet' and 'none of this means', and keep the author's own judgements separate from facts and from the words of people the author quotes.
paragraphs: On a calm morning off the coast of a small island in the Gulf of Thailand, a team of volunteer divers hangs fragments of staghorn coral from what look like underwater washing lines. Within a year, if all goes well, each fragment will have grown large enough to be cemented onto a damaged section of reef. Scenes like this have become a staple of conservation fundraising, and it is easy to see why: few images of environmental action are as hopeful, or as photogenic, as a diver tending a nursery of young corals. Yet the popularity of coral gardening deserves far closer scrutiny than it usually receives.

The case for intervention is, admittedly, a strong one. Reefs cover well under one per cent of the ocean floor but support roughly a quarter of all marine species, and they protect coastlines from storm waves while sustaining the fisheries and tourism on which millions of people depend. Repeated marine heatwaves have caused mass bleaching events, in which stressed corals expel the algae that supply most of their food and, if temperatures stay high, gradually starve. Where reefs have been reduced to rubble, natural recovery can take decades, and in some places it may not happen at all. Against this background, the impulse to lend nature a helping hand is entirely understandable.

Restoration projects now take several forms. The most common involves growing fragments in nurseries before 'outplanting' them onto the reef. Other groups stabilise loose rubble with metal frames so that coral larvae have somewhere to settle, or collect spawn during the annual mass release of eggs and rear the larvae in tanks. More ambitious researchers are attempting what is sometimes called assisted evolution, selectively breeding corals that appear to tolerate higher temperatures. Each approach has produced genuine successes at particular sites, and the best-run projects report that more than half of their outplanted fragments survive for at least two years.

The difficulty is one of scale, and it is a difficulty that promotional material rarely mentions. A 2024 review by marine scientists at a university in southern Thailand estimated that the combined area restored by all projects in the region over the previous decade amounted to less than two square kilometres, a figure dwarfed by the area lost in a single bleaching season. Restoring a reef one fragment at a time is, in the review's memorable phrase, 'like replanting a forest with a teaspoon'. To my mind, this comparison is, if anything, too generous, because a replanted forest is not routinely cooked by the next heatwave.

Equally troubling is the way in which success is often measured. Many projects count the number of fragments planted, a figure that is easy to report to donors but says little about whether a functioning reef is returning. Survival rates are frequently recorded for only a few months, and the fish, invertebrates and complex three-dimensional structure that make a reef valuable are seldom monitored at all. Dr. Kanya Sirimongkol, who has advised several restoration groups, puts it bluntly: 'We have become very good at counting corals and rather poor at asking whether we have rebuilt anything.' It would be unfair to blame volunteers for this; short funding cycles reward visible activity rather than patient measurement.

None of this means that restoration is futile. On small, carefully chosen sites, such as a reef that shelters a village harbour or one that attracts the divers on whom a local economy depends, targeted planting may buy valuable time. Nurseries can also serve as living gene banks, preserving varieties that might otherwise disappear before heat-tolerant strains can be identified. And projects that involve local fishers and schoolchildren may build a constituency for marine protection that outlasts any individual planting. Such projects also generate practical knowledge about which species and techniques suit local conditions, knowledge that may prove invaluable if ocean warming is eventually brought under control.

What restoration cannot do is substitute for the measures that would allow reefs to survive in the first place: reducing the greenhouse gas emissions that drive ocean warming, and controlling the overfishing and coastal pollution that leave corals less able to withstand heat. The real danger is not that coral gardening fails, but that its success stories allow governments and corporations to appear active while postponing harder decisions. A diver holding a coral fragment makes a fine photograph. It should not be mistaken for a policy.

questions.q: Why does the author begin the article by describing divers hanging coral fragments on underwater lines?
options: to explain step by step how a coral nursery is constructed
to introduce an appealing image that the article will go on to question
to show that volunteers achieve better results than trained scientists
to persuade readers to join a coral restoration project as volunteers
questions.explain: ¶1 จบด้วย “Yet the popularity of coral gardening deserves far closer scrutiny than it usually receives” แสดงว่าภาพที่สวยงามตอนต้นถูกยกมาเพื่อนำไปสู่การตั้งคำถาม (B) ตัวเลือก A เป็นกับดักเพราะย่อหน้ามีรายละเอียดการแขวนกิ่งปะการังจริง แต่ไม่ได้อธิบายวิธีสร้างเป็นขั้นตอน และไม่ใช่จุดประสงค์หลัก ส่วน D ขัดกับน้ำเสียงเชิงตั้งข้อสงสัยของผู้เขียน

questions.q: The word 'staple' in paragraph 1 is closest in meaning to
options: a regular and standard feature
a small metal fastener for paper
a basic food eaten every day
an unusual and rare exception
questions.explain: ¶1: “Scenes like this have become a staple of conservation fundraising, and it is easy to see why” ในบริบทนี้ staple หมายถึงสิ่งที่พบเป็นประจำ/องค์ประกอบมาตรฐาน (A) ตัวเลือก B และ C เป็นความหมายอื่นของคำเดียวกัน (ลวดเย็บกระดาษ, อาหารหลัก) ที่ไม่เข้ากับบริบทการระดมทุน

questions.q: In paragraph 2, the author's attitude towards 'the impulse to lend nature a helping hand' is best described as
options: critical, because the author considers such efforts naive
indifferent, because the author is interested only in statistics
sympathetic, while signalling that reservations are to follow
wholeheartedly supportive, without any form of qualification
questions.explain: ¶2 เปิดด้วย “The case for intervention is, admittedly, a strong one” และปิดด้วย “entirely understandable” คำว่า admittedly บอกว่าผู้เขียนยอมรับเหตุผลนี้ แต่กำลังจะแย้งต่อ จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก D เป็นกับดักเพราะคำว่า “entirely understandable” ฟังดูสนับสนุนเต็มที่ แต่ “understandable” ไม่เท่ากับ 'supportive' และบทความวิจารณ์ต่อใน ¶4–5

questions.q: According to paragraph 3, 'assisted evolution' refers to
options: rearing larvae collected during the corals' yearly mass spawning
fixing loose rubble with frames so that young corals can settle
moving fragments from warm reefs to cooler waters further north
breeding corals selectively for their apparent tolerance of heat
questions.explain: ¶3: “assisted evolution, selectively breeding corals that appear to tolerate higher temperatures” ตรงกับ D ซึ่งถอดความใหม่ ตัวเลือก A และ B เป็นวิธีฟื้นฟูอีกแบบที่อยู่ในย่อหน้าเดียวกัน จึงเป็นกับดักสำหรับผู้ที่อ่านไม่ละเอียด

questions.q: Which of the following is presented in paragraph 4 as the author's own view rather than as a finding or wording of the 2024 review?
options: The area restored in the region over ten years was under two square kilometres.
Rebuilding a reef fragment by fragment is like replanting a forest with a teaspoon.
The comparison between a reef and a forest actually understates the problem.
The review was carried out by marine scientists at a university in southern Thailand.
questions.explain: ¶4: “To my mind, this comparison is, if anything, too generous” วลี to my mind แสดงความเห็นส่วนตัวของผู้เขียน จึงตอบ C ตัวเลือก B เป็นกับดักที่สุด เพราะการเปรียบเทียบกับช้อนชาเป็นถ้อยคำของงานทบทวน (“in the review's memorable phrase”) ไม่ใช่ของผู้เขียน ส่วน A เป็นตัวเลขที่งานทบทวนประมาณการไว้

questions.q: Why does the author quote Dr. Kanya Sirimongkol in paragraph 5?
options: to support the claim that projects measure activity rather than real recovery
to show that experts strongly disagree about whether restoration has value
to place the blame for poor monitoring on untrained volunteer divers
to provide new survival figures for fragments planted on damaged reefs
questions.explain: ¶5: คำพูด “We have become very good at counting corals and rather poor at asking whether we have rebuilt anything” สนับสนุนประเด็นของย่อหน้าที่ว่าโครงการนับจำนวนกิ่งปะการังแต่ไม่ได้วัดการฟื้นตัวจริง (A) ตัวเลือก C ขัดกับที่ผู้เขียนบอกว่า “It would be unfair to blame volunteers for this”

questions.q: It can be inferred from paragraph 5 that many projects report the number of fragments planted mainly because
options: it is the most reliable indicator that a healthy reef is returning
it is a simple, visible figure that suits short-term funding
volunteers lack the training needed to count fish and invertebrates
donors do not permit monitoring that lasts longer than a few months
questions.explain: ¶5: ตัวเลขนี้ “is easy to report to donors” และ “short funding cycles reward visible activity rather than patient measurement” จึงอนุมานได้ว่าเหตุผลคือเป็นตัวเลขง่าย ๆ ที่เห็นผลชัดและเหมาะกับทุนระยะสั้น (B) ตัวเลือก A ขัดกับข้อความว่าตัวเลขนี้ “says little about whether a functioning reef is returning” ส่วน D เกินกว่าที่บทความกล่าว

questions.q: What is the function of paragraph 6 in the author's argument?
options: It abandons the earlier criticism in favour of a wholly positive view.
It presents evidence that restoration already works at a regional scale.
It describes the historical development of restoration in Thailand.
It qualifies the earlier criticism by identifying where restoration is worthwhile.
questions.explain: ¶6 เริ่มด้วย “None of this means that restoration is futile” แล้วยกกรณีที่การฟื้นฟูมีประโยชน์ เช่นแนวปะการังเล็ก ๆ ที่เลือกอย่างระมัดระวังและธนาคารพันธุกรรม จึงเป็นการจำกัดขอบเขตคำวิจารณ์ (D) ตัวเลือก A เป็นกับดักเพราะผู้เขียนไม่ได้ละทิ้งคำวิจารณ์ ซึ่งกลับมาอีกใน ¶7 ส่วน B ขัดกับปัญหาเรื่องขนาดใน ¶4

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the author's overall stance on coral restoration?
options: conditionally supportive, but wary of its use as a substitute for deeper action
broadly hostile, regarding restoration as harmful to the reefs it targets
cautiously optimistic that restoration will eventually match reef losses
frustrated mainly by volunteers who lack proper scientific training
questions.explain: ผู้เขียนยอมรับคุณค่าในบางกรณี (¶6) แต่เตือนใน ¶7 ว่า “What restoration cannot do is substitute for the measures that would allow reefs to survive” และ “It should not be mistaken for a policy” จึงตอบ A ตัวเลือก C ขัดกับ ¶4 ที่ชี้ว่าพื้นที่ฟื้นฟูเล็กมากเมื่อเทียบกับที่เสียไป ส่วน B เกินจริงเพราะผู้เขียนไม่ได้บอกว่าการฟื้นฟูเป็นอันตราย

questions.q: What do stressed corals expel during a bleaching event? (Answer in NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶2: “stressed corals expel the algae that supply most of their food” คำตอบคือ (the) algae (สาหร่ายที่อาศัยอยู่ในปะการัง)

questions.q: What term is used for moving nursery-grown fragments onto the reef? (Answer in ONE WORD from the passage.)
questions.explain: ¶3: “growing fragments in nurseries before 'outplanting' them onto the reef” คำตอบคือ outplanting

questions.q: Apart from buying time, what can nurseries serve as, according to paragraph 6? (Answer in NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS from the passage.)

title: Inoculating the Mind: The Promise and Limits of Prebunking
skill_tip_en: Find the exact sentence the question points to, then choose the option that keeps its meaning in different words; distrust options that copy the passage's wording but change who, when, how much or why.
paragraphs: Efforts to counter misinformation have traditionally taken the form of correction. Once a false claim begins to circulate, journalists, fact-checkers and public agencies set out to debunk it, publishing evidence that contradicts it. Although such corrections can reduce belief in specific falsehoods, they suffer from a structural disadvantage: they almost always arrive after the claim has spread, and they rarely reach everyone who saw the original. Many fact-checkers themselves acknowledge this limitation, describing their work as a race against falsehoods that they are unlikely ever to win. A growing body of research has therefore explored a complementary strategy, known as prebunking, which aims to build resistance to misleading content before people encounter it.

The idea draws on inoculation theory, a framework developed by social psychologists in the 1960s. Just as a vaccine exposes the immune system to a weakened form of a virus, psychological inoculation exposes people to a weakened dose of a persuasive attack, together with a clear explanation of why it is misleading. The theory holds that this experience prompts people to generate their own counter-arguments, so that when they meet the full-strength version later, they are better equipped to resist it. The aim, in other words, is not to prevent exposure altogether but to render it harmless. Early studies focused on specific claims, but this approach was limited by an obvious problem: no one can predict every falsehood that will appear.

Recent work has therefore shifted from inoculating against particular claims to inoculating against the techniques that misinformation commonly employs. These include emotionally manipulative language, false dichotomies that present only two options when more exist, the scapegoating of individuals or groups, and the use of fake experts to lend a claim an air of authority. Because such techniques recur across topics as different as vaccines, elections and investment fraud, teaching people to recognise them could, in principle, offer broad protection from a single intervention.

Evidence for this technique-based approach is encouraging. In a 2024 experiment at a university in central Thailand, Dr. Siriporn Thammasak and her team asked 1,800 adults to watch either a 90-second animated video explaining the 'fake expert' technique or a neutral video of similar length about household recycling. Participants were then shown a series of social media posts, some of which used the technique. Those who had watched the prebunking video were about 20 per cent better at identifying manipulative posts and reported being less willing to share them. Notably, the size of the effect did not depend on participants' political views or level of education.

Nevertheless, the approach has clear limitations. The protective effect appears to decay over time; in several studies, it had weakened substantially within a month unless participants received a short 'booster' reminder. Laboratory measures may also overstate real-world impact, since identifying a manipulative post in a survey is not the same as resisting one in a fast-moving feed, where attention is divided and content arrives from trusted friends. Some researchers have further warned that poorly designed interventions might breed general cynicism, leading people to distrust accurate information as readily as false claims. One study that found improved detection of misleading posts, for instance, also recorded a small decline in trust towards reliable news outlets.

There are also practical and ethical questions about delivery. The most ambitious trials have placed prebunking videos in the advertising slots of video-sharing platforms, reaching millions of viewers at low cost. Critics point out, however, that this places considerable influence in the hands of private companies, and that decisions about which techniques count as manipulative are not always politically neutral. Prebunking delivered through schools and public libraries may command greater trust, although it reaches far fewer people and depends on the willingness of teachers to adopt it. There is also a risk that audiences who realise a video has been paid for will dismiss its message as a form of propaganda.

On balance, prebunking seems best understood not as a replacement for fact-checking but as one layer in a wider defence. It is relatively cheap, scalable and applicable across topics, qualities that corrections lack. Yet its benefits are modest and short-lived, and its effectiveness outside controlled settings remains uncertain. A sensible strategy would combine prebunking with timely corrections, changes to platform design that slow the spread of viral content, and long-term investment in media literacy, so that resistance to manipulation becomes a lasting habit rather than the brief effect of a single video.

title: Money With No Strings: What Basic Income Trials Can and Cannot Tell Us
skill_tip_en: For NOT or EXCEPT questions, match each option to a specific sentence in the passage; the answer is the option you cannot find, even if it sounds true in the real world.
paragraphs: Few policy ideas have travelled as quickly from the margins to the mainstream as universal basic income: a regular cash payment made to every individual, without conditions and regardless of whether they work. Supporters argue that it could reduce poverty more efficiently than existing welfare systems, provide security in an economy disrupted by automation, and free people to pursue education, care or small enterprises. Critics counter that it would be prohibitively expensive and might discourage paid work. Because the debate has often been conducted in abstract terms, researchers and governments have increasingly turned to field trials in the hope of settling it with evidence.

Strictly speaking, few of these experiments test a universal basic income at all. Most provide payments to a limited group selected by lottery or by income, for a fixed period of one to three years, and fund them through charities or research grants rather than taxation. A typical design, such as a 2022 pilot in two districts of north-eastern Thailand led by Dr. Anan Phromsuwan, gave 1,200 low-income adults a monthly payment of 2,000 baht for two years and compared their outcomes with those of a similar group who received nothing. Participants were free to spend the money as they wished, and researchers tracked their employment, health, debts and spending through surveys every six months. Such trials can reveal how individuals respond to unconditional cash, but they cannot show what would happen if an entire population received it.

Within these constraints, the findings have been fairly consistent. Contrary to the fears of critics, recipients rarely reduce their working hours by much. In the Thai pilot, average weekly hours of paid work fell by less than one hour, and the decline was concentrated among two groups: mothers of young children and young adults who had returned to education. Recipients also reported lower levels of stress and were less likely to take out high-interest loans from informal moneylenders. Spending on alcohol and tobacco, a frequent concern among sceptics, did not increase; if anything, it fell slightly.

Some effects, however, were weaker than advocates had predicted. There was little evidence that the payments led recipients to start businesses in large numbers, and improvements in physical health were small and statistically uncertain. Several trials elsewhere have reported similar results, and some researchers suggest that a payment known to end after two years is unlikely to change long-term decisions, such as whether to take the risk of setting up a firm. Advocates had expected that relief from immediate financial pressure would encourage experimentation, but the data offered little support for that hope. People who expect their income to stop may quite sensibly treat the money as a temporary cushion rather than as a foundation for new plans.

This points to a more fundamental difficulty. Temporary, partial trials cannot capture the economy-wide effects that matter most in the policy debate. A permanent national scheme would have to be financed, most likely through higher taxes, which might themselves influence how much people choose to work. It could raise demand for goods and services in poor areas, and potentially prices as well. It might also alter social expectations about work, family and community in ways that no two-year experiment involving a few thousand people could detect. Economists describe these as general equilibrium effects, and they are notoriously difficult to estimate.

There are ethical complications too. Selecting some families by lottery to receive money while their neighbours receive none can create resentment, and in one pilot, local officials reported tensions at village meetings. Researchers must also decide what happens when a trial ends. Recipients who have adjusted their household budgets around a regular payment may face genuine hardship when it stops, which has led some ethics committees to require gradual phase-out periods rather than an abrupt end to payments.

None of this makes trials worthless. They have usefully dispelled some of the more alarming predictions about idleness and wasteful spending, and they offer valuable evidence about the design of targeted cash transfers, which many governments already operate. What they cannot do is answer the central political question of whether a universal scheme is affordable and desirable. That question involves judgements about fairness, the proper role of the state and the value of work, which evidence can inform but never entirely resolve. Trials, in this sense, are best seen as one contribution to a wider public deliberation rather than as a final verdict.

title: Beyond the Burger: The Uneven Rise of Alternative Proteins
skill_tip_en: Before answering organisation or purpose questions, label each paragraph in two or three words (example, cause, category, obstacle, conclusion) and ask what job it does for the article as a whole.
paragraphs: In a busy food court in central Bangkok, a stall that opened two years ago sells what looks, smells and very nearly tastes like minced pork stir-fried with holy basil. The 'pork', however, is made from soy protein, coconut fat and a yeast extract that supplies the savoury depth customers expect. The stall's owner says that roughly one in five of her lunchtime customers now chooses the plant-based version, most of them not vegetarians but office workers who are 'trying to eat a bit less meat'. Her experience captures, on a small scale, both the promise of alternative proteins and the questions that continue to surround them.

The case for such products rests largely on the environmental footprint of conventional livestock. Raising animals for meat and milk occupies a large share of the world's agricultural land, consumes vast quantities of water and feed, and is responsible for a significant proportion of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly the methane released by cattle. As incomes rise across Asia and Africa, global demand for meat is projected to keep growing for decades. Proponents argue that unless at least part of that demand can be met in other ways, it will be difficult to reconcile food security with climate targets.

The most established alternatives are plant-based products, which combine proteins from soy, peas, wheat or mung beans with fats and flavourings to imitate the texture and taste of meat. In many ways, these are refinements of a very old tradition: tofu, tempeh and wheat gluten have been eaten across East and Southeast Asia for centuries. What is new is the ambition to replicate specific animal products closely enough to persuade committed meat-eaters to switch. Sales grew rapidly in the late 2010s, but in several Western markets they have since levelled off, as early curiosity has given way to concerns about price and taste.

A second, more experimental category is cultivated meat, produced by growing animal cells in large steel vessels known as bioreactors. In principle, this would deliver genuine meat without the need to raise and slaughter animals. In practice, the technology faces formidable obstacles. The nutrient solutions in which the cells are grown have been expensive, and scaling production from laboratory flasks to industrial volumes has proved far harder than early investors anticipated. Only a handful of countries have so far approved cultivated meat for sale, and the quantities available remain tiny. Questions about how such products should be labelled, and whether consumers will accept meat grown in a factory, also remain unresolved.

Between these two lie fermentation-based proteins. Some companies use microorganisms such as fungi to produce protein-rich biomass directly; others engineer yeasts to manufacture specific ingredients, such as the milk protein that makes cheese melt and stretch. Fermentation has the advantage of relying on equipment and expertise already used in brewing and food processing, which may allow it to expand more quickly than cultivated meat. Insects, meanwhile, represent an alternative that is novel mainly to Western consumers. In north-eastern Thailand, crickets and silkworm pupae have long been sold as snacks, and cricket farming has grown into a modest commercial industry supplying flour for protein bars and animal feed.

Despite this variety, the sector faces several common hurdles. Price is the most obvious: most alternatives still cost more than the cheapest conventional meat, which benefits from decades of efficiency gains and, in many countries, public subsidies. Taste and texture matter as well, since many consumers who try a product once do not buy it again. Cultural attachment to meat, particularly at festivals and family celebrations, is a further barrier that no amount of technical improvement can easily remove. There is also a growing debate about health. Critics argue that some plant-based products are highly processed and high in salt, while defenders reply that they compare favourably with the sausages and burgers they are designed to replace.

Perhaps the most important lesson, then, is that alternative proteins are unlikely to replace meat in a single, dramatic shift. A more plausible future is one of gradual blending, in which conventional meat is partly substituted in everyday dishes, alternative ingredients are mixed into familiar foods, and the choice between them depends on price, culture and occasion. The Bangkok stall owner, who still sells far more pork than plant-based mince, would probably agree. 'People don't want a revolution,' she says. 'They want lunch.'
